before: A comparison asks a question. >= means greater than or equal to. In C a comparison produces int 1 when true and 0 when false.
if (condition) runs its block for a nonzero condition. else runs its alternative when the condition is zero.
int seats = 2; gives seats a value. seats >= 2 checks that value without changing it. == is an equality comparison; a single = would be assignment.
Only one block of this if/else pair runs. An exact boundary of 2 passes >= 2 but would not pass > 2.
after: A comparison checks two values. `seats >= 2` asks whether seats is at least 2. C gives this comparison the value 1 for true or 0 for false.
A condition decides which path runs. `if` runs its braces when the condition is nonzero. `else` runs its braces when the condition is zero.
Reading seats in a comparison does not change it. `==` checks whether two values are equal. A single `=` stores a value instead.
Only one path in this if/else pair runs. The `>=` sign includes the boundary: 2 is enough. The `>` sign would require more than 2.
